title: Air Force Academy Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Air Force Academy wells have a 296 ft median depth, 11.1 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $20,800-$32,700.
h1: Air Force Academy Colorado Well Reports
intro_html:
Well records within five miles of Air Force Academy show a wide range of conditions. Among 1,862 permitted wells, 993 report a total depth and 454 report a pump yield, so the available records are useful but not complete for every property.

The local pattern is mainly Denver Basin and fractured-bedrock drilling. Most permits are for domestic or household use, and neighboring wells can help frame a bid, expected production, and water-level risk before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Air Force Academy well depth: plan for a variable hole
sections.html:
The median reported well depth is 296 feet. The middle half runs from 195 to 422 feet, meaning a bid based only on the median can miss the actual drilling conditions on a particular lot. Ten percent of reported wells reach 600 feet or more, and the deepest record is 2,290 feet.

Depth is spread across the area: 11% are under 100 feet, 39% are 100-300 feet, and 40% are 300-600 feet. Permits name unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, with Denver and Arapahoe aquifers also represented. Sedimentary Denver Basin material and fractured rock can change quickly from one location to the next, so nearby well logs matter more than a countywide assumption.

sections.heading: Expected well yield near Gleneagle and Monument
sections.html:
Reported production is generally workable for a household, but the records do not describe every permitted well. The median pump yield is 11.1 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 9.0 to 14.2 gallons per minute. Seventy-two percent of reported yields fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 24% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute in this dataset, and 4% are in the 1-5 gallon-per-minute range. That does not guarantee a strong well on an untested parcel. Ask for the neighboring well construction, pumping test, storage setup, and permitted use. A licensed driller can also explain how casing, grout, pump size, and storage affect the usable supply.

sections.heading: Water levels show a deeper recent measurement
sections.html:
Among the 78 records reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 200 feet. The middle half ranges from 95 to 299 feet below the surface. That is a substantial depth for pump design, trenching, and electrical planning, even before the well reaches its total depth.

The decade series moves from a median of 132 feet below surface in the 1970s to 200 feet in the 2010s and 240 feet in the 2020s. The series suggests deeper measured water levels over time, but it is not a complete monitoring record and includes different wells and locations. Treat it as a caution for pump sizing and due diligence, not proof that every local water table is dropping uniformly.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Air Force Academy
sections.html:
Permit activity is concentrated in the late twentieth century. The records show 34 permits in the 1950s, 23 in the 1960s, 218 in the 1970s, 279 in the 1980s, and 428 in the 1990s. Activity then totals 171 permits in the 2000s, 132 in the 2010s, and 77 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

The most frequently recorded drillers are Fletcher Drilling, also listed as Fletcher, Thomas, with 169 wells; W. V. Harding & Sons, listed as Harding, Fred E., with 118; and Hamacher Well Works Inc, listed as Hamacher, Alan Ray, with 114. These records identify local history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and warranty before hiring.

sections.heading: Air Force Academy well drilling cost estimate
sections.html:
The cost model for this area uses a typical drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 296-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $14,800-$20,700. That is only the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,800-$32,700 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median hole can exceed that range, particularly where a site requires difficult access, extra casing, or more pumping equipment. Get a written proposal that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, permits, trenching, electrical, and any dry-hole terms.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Water quality deserves specific attention here. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 91 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 19 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not establish contamination on a particular parcel, but they are a reason to review local records and test an existing well before closing.

Low yield and dry-hole risk remain separate from water quality. A permit record does not guarantee that a well is productive today. Check the well construction, pump test, static level, maintenance history, and laboratory results. Also confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, access for drilling equipment, and the building department's requirements for a new home. An augmentation plan may be relevant in an over-appropriated basin, depending on the proposed use and permit.

sections.heading: A practical lot review for Palmer Lake and nearby areas
sections.html:
Before committing to land near Air Force Academy, compare several neighboring permits rather than relying on one successful well. Look at total depth, aquifer name, static water level, yield, construction details, and the age of each record. The same approach is useful in Gleneagle, Monument, Woodmoor, Cascade-Chipita Park, Palmer Lake, and Green Mountain Falls.

For a buildable lot, confirm legal water use first, then price the well, pump, storage, power, trenching, and septic work together. If the property has an existing well, collect a current water-quality sample and have the system inspected. For a new well, ask the driller how the bid changes if the hole passes the local depth range. A water-rights professional can address household use, augmentation, and any restrictions tied to the permit.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Air Force Academy, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 296 feet, and the middle half of reported wells is 195-422 feet. Forty percent are 300-600 feet, while 10% reach 600 feet or more. The deepest record is 2,290 feet. Actual depth can vary substantially because permits name both Denver Basin and fractured-bedrock conditions.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Air Force Academy?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 296-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $14,800-$20,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,800-$32,700. A written bid should clarify casing, grout, testing, access, and dry-hole terms.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Air Force Academy produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 11.1 gallons per minute, with a middle half of 9.0-14.2 gallons per minute. Seventy-two percent of reported yields are 5-15 gallons per minute, and 24% exceed 15 gallons per minute. These figures come from 454 records, so they do not guarantee production on a new lot.

faq.q: Is well water near Air Force Academy safe to drink?
faq.a: The permit map includes 91 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 19 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not prove a specific well is unsafe. Test an existing or new well through a qualified laboratory, review nearby environmental records, and use treatment if results require it.

faq.q: Are water levels getting lower near Air Force Academy?
faq.a: The available series shows median static water levels at 132 feet below surface in the 1970s, 200 feet in the 2010s, and 240 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels over time, but only 78 records report static levels and the wells differ by location. Use the trend for caution, not as proof of uniform decline.
